# How to use Qwen Chat to create personalised study flashcards for any subject

**Hook:** By the end of this guide, you'll be able to paste in your study notes, ask Qwen (Alibaba's AI assistant) to turn them into question-and-answer flashcards, and then copy them into whatever quiz tool you already use — so revising takes a fraction of the usual time. This is for anyone studying for an exam, picking up a new skill, or just trying to remember things better.

## Before you start
- **An account at chat.qwen.ai.** You can sign in with a Google account, a GitHub account, or an email address — pick whichever you already use. A free plan is available and is enough for this task.
- **A device with a browser** (laptop, tablet or phone). Qwen Chat is web-based, so no install is required.
- **Some study material to work from.** A few paragraphs of notes, a chapter summary, or even a short topic description is plenty. The more specific your notes, the better the cards.
- **Roughly 10–15 minutes.** Most of that time is reading and picking the cards you want to keep.

## Step 1 — Open Qwen Chat and start a fresh conversation
Open your browser, go to **chat.qwen.ai**, and sign in if you aren't already. Once you're on the main chat screen, look for a button like **"New Chat"** (often a small **+** icon or a pencil symbol near the top or left side of the page). Click it. A blank conversation box opens, ready for your message. Starting a new chat each time keeps earlier topics from confusing the AI, which is important because a long, mixed conversation tends to make answers less focused. **If it looks different:** if you can't find a "New Chat" button, just type your request into whatever text box is visible — Qwen will treat it as the start of a new thread on its end. **You'll know it worked when** the screen shows an empty message field with no previous conversation visible.

## Step 2 — Tell Qwen what subject you're studying and paste in your notes
Type a short intro that says (a) the topic, (b) roughly what level you're at, and (c) the notes you want turned into cards. Then press **Enter** or tap the send arrow. Qwen will read your message and start processing it. This first message is where you set the "frame" — the more clearly you describe the subject, the more on-target the flashcards will be. **If it looks different:** if your notes are very long, consider pasting just one section at a time so Qwen doesn't have to skim anything important. **You'll know it worked when** Qwen replies by acknowledging the topic and confirming what it's about to do.

💬 Example: *"Hi Qwen — I'm studying for a Year 9 biology exam on cell structure. Here's my notes: [paste your notes here, or describe: 'The main topics are animal cells vs plant cells, the function of the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cell membrane, and how osmosis works.' Please make 12 flashcards covering these."*

## Step 3 — Ask Qwen to format each flashcard clearly
In the same conversation, send a second message asking Qwen to lay out every flashcard in a consistent format — usually **"Question: … / Answer: …"** on separate lines, with a number in front of each one. Press send and wait a few seconds. Qwen will re-format its previous answers into a clean list you can easily copy. A consistent layout saves you time later because you can paste the whole block into a spreadsheet or a flashcard app without re-typing anything. **If it looks different:** if Qwen gives you a paragraph instead of a list, just reply with *"Please list them numbered, with Question and Answer on separate lines."* — it will happily redo them. **You'll know it worked when** the response is a numbered list where each item has a clear "Question" line and an "Answer" line.

💬 Example: *"Great, please rewrite those as a numbered list, with each one formatted exactly like this: 'Card 1 — Question: [question] | Answer: [answer]'. Use a vertical bar to separate Q and A so I can copy them straight into a spreadsheet."*

## Step 4 — Ask for more cards, harder cards, or a quick quiz check
Now send another short message asking Qwen to either (a) generate **more cards** on the same topic, (b) make the existing cards **harder** (for example, "give me application-level questions, not just definitions"), or (c) **quiz you** by hiding the answers and asking the questions one at a time. This is where Qwen really shines as a study partner — you can keep refining the same set until it matches your exam style. **If it looks different:** the "quiz me" option is just a chat request; there's no special button. **You'll know it worked when** Qwen either produces a longer list, asks you a question, or offers a "harder" version of the same cards.

💬 Example: *"Please add 6 more cards, but make them harder — focus on application and 'why' questions rather than simple definitions. Then quiz me on the first 5 cards one at a time."*

## Step 5 — Copy the flashcard list out of Qwen
Scroll back up to the formatted list and **select the text** with your mouse, then copy it (**Ctrl+C** on Windows/Linux, **Cmd+C** on Mac, or long-press on mobile). Open the place you want to study from — Google Sheets, Notion, a notes app, or a flashcard app like Anki or Quizlet — and paste it in. Qwen doesn't store your cards in a built-in flashcard deck, so this copy step is the bridge between the AI's output and your study routine. **If it looks different:** on mobile, you may need to tap-and-hold inside Qwen's response to bring up a "Copy" or "Select all" option. **You'll know it worked when** the flashcards appear as editable text in your chosen app, ready to import or tweak.

## Step 6 — Test yourself, then come back and refine weak cards
Spend a few minutes quizzing yourself with the cards you just saved. Notice which ones you got wrong, felt fuzzy on, or found too easy. Then **return to your Qwen chat** and ask it to focus on exactly those weak spots — for example, *"Give me 5 more cards that drill the difference between osmosis and diffusion, because I keep mixing them up."* This feedback loop is what makes AI-generated flashcards genuinely useful: the set evolves with your understanding, instead of staying static like a textbook chapter. **If it looks different:** if Qwen has lost the thread of your earlier messages, just paste in your original topic description again as a refresher. **You'll know it worked when** you can identify at least 3 cards that you now answer confidently, and a short list of topics you still want to drill.

💬 Example: *"I got these wrong: [list 2-3 topics]. Please make 4 more cards on those specific points, and include a tiny hint on the back of each one."*

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting a 50-page textbook and expecting perfect cards.** Qwen works best when you give it focused chunks of notes or a clear topic summary. **Fix:** paste one section at a time, or describe the key concepts in your own words first.
- **Skipping the "format" step.** If you don't ask for a numbered "Question / Answer" layout, you'll get a paragraph that's painful to copy into anything. **Fix:** always send the second message asking for the exact format you want.
- **Treating AI cards as automatically correct.** Qwen can occasionally get a fact subtly wrong, especially for niche subjects. **Fix:** spot-check the first 5 cards against your actual textbook or syllabus before you commit to the whole set.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** any time you need to remember a list — countries and capitals, foreign vocabulary, recipe ratios — you can spin up a quick flashcard set in minutes instead of handwriting them.
- **For your study or exams:** you get a personalised revision deck that adapts to *your* notes, not a generic one from the internet, and you can ask for harder questions as the exam gets closer.
- **If you're just getting started:** don't overthink it — pick one small topic, run through the six steps above once, and you'll have the hang of it by the second subject.

## Try it now
Open **chat.qwen.ai**, start a new chat, and paste in this exact message to make your first set of cards right now:

> *"Please create 8 flashcards covering the basics of [your subject — e.g. 'the solar system', 'French food vocabulary', 'intro to spreadsheets']. Format each one as: 'Card N — Question: ... | Answer: ...'. Keep answers under 20 words."*

Two minutes from now you'll have a deck you can copy into your favourite notes app and start quizzing yourself tonight.
